tip: Yes/no questions use a separate word 'mu': 'biliyor musunuz' (do you know). The person ending -sunuz rides on 'musunuz', not on 'biliyor'.
'kimse' (nobody) still needs a negative verb: 'dinlemiyor' (isn't listening). Turkish doubles the negative where English uses just one.
'içerim' uses the -er ending for habits and general facts: iç + er + im. Use it for what you usually do, not -iyor for right now.
Future is stem + -ecek + person: 'özleyeceğim' (I will miss). A 'y' slips in as a buffer because 'özle' ends in a vowel.
'okuyorsun' (an -iyor form) covers both you are reading now and you read generally. The -iyor form does not split habit from ongoing action.
'yapmayı' = yap + ma (turns the verb into a noun, doing) + yı (object marker). 'sever' needs its object marked this way.
'kızım' = kız + ım (my daughter). Turkish usually has no separate word for my, you attach the owner onto the noun.
'evin çatısı' is an of-chain: 'evin' (of the house) plus 'çatısı' (its roof). Both the owner and the thing take a suffix.
'değil' negates nouns and adjectives, not verbs: 'haklı değilsiniz' (you are not right). The person ending sits on 'değilsiniz'.
'önerir misiniz' pairs the -ir ending with the question word 'mi' for a polite request, close to English would you recommend.
'hastayı' carries -yı because it is a specific, known object: the patient. A plain 'hasta' would mean just any patient.
Turkish says 'yağmur yağıyor' (rain is raining), the noun and verb built from the same root. Standard way to say it is raining.
'hiç' means at all only when the verb is negative: 'hiç tanımıyorum' (do not know at all). It leans on the negative verb.
'sürüyor' shows -iyor echoing the root vowel: 'sür' has 'ü', so the suffix rounds to -üyor, not -iyor.
'yağmur var' = there is rain. 'var' means there is or there are and needs no verb for to be. Its opposite is 'yok'.
'kapalıydı' = 'kapalı' (closed) + ydı (was). Adding -(y)dı to an adjective puts it in the past, no separate verb needed.
'konuşamıyorum' means I cannot speak. The -amı- inside is the negative of ability, the opposite of -abil (can).
'düşünmem lazım' = I need to think. Verb plus -mem or -mam plus 'lazım' is the everyday way to say I have to.
'izledik' = izle + dik (we watched). Past tense adds -di plus a person ending, here -dik for we.
'Türkiye'deki' means the ones in Turkey. The -ki after a location turns it into an adjective describing the next noun.
'eşimle' = eş + im + le (with my spouse). The ending -le or -la attached to a noun means with.
Many Turkish greetings take the plural -lar: 'akşamlar' (evenings), not singular 'akşam'. Same pattern shows up in 'iyi geceler'.
'tamir etti' = fixed. Many actions are a noun plus 'etmek': 'tamir' (repair) plus 'etti' (did). The noun stays put, 'etmek' carries tense.
'yapmadan önce' = before doing. Verb plus -madan önce means before X-ing: 'yapmadan önce' (before mopping).
'konuşabilir' = can speak: konuş + abilir. The -abilir or -ebilir slotted onto the root means able to.
'yemekten' takes -ten, not -den, because 'yemek' ends in a voiceless 'k'. After voiceless consonants the from ending hardens.
'okurken' = while reading. The ending -ken means while and attaches straight onto the verb form.
'yürüyüşe' = yürüyüş + e (for a walk). The -e or -a ending marks where you are heading or aiming.
'başlamak' wants the -e ending, so it is 'işe başlamak' (start work), not the object form. The verb decides the ending.
'seni' = sen + i, the object form of you. The -i ending marks the definite object of 'düşünüyoruz' (we are thinking of).
